title: From Triumph to Tragedy
summary: In 1989 crowds breached the Berlin Wall as communist regimes across eastern Europe peacefully collapsed, and by the end of 1991 the Soviet Union itself had dissolved into fifteen nations. The Cold War's end left the United States the world's lone superpower, and President George H. W. Bush proclaimed a 'new world order.' He intervened in Panama and, in 1991, led an international coalition in the Gulf War that expelled Iraq from Kuwait. But a recession undercut Bush's soaring popularity, and in 1992 Bill Clinton—blending social liberalism with promises to shrink government and reform welfare—won a three-way race in which Ross Perot took nearly a fifth of the vote.

Clinton pushed NAFTA through Congress in 1993 and expanded the Earned Income Tax Credit, but his ambitious health-care plan collapsed, and in 1994 Newt Gingrich's 'Contract with America' Republicans captured Congress. Clinton recovered by co-opting conservative themes, declaring 'the era of big government is over' and signing the 1996 abolition of AFDC welfare. A booming economy—driven by computers, the Internet, and globalization—produced low unemployment and budget surpluses, though inequality widened, the dot-com bubble eventually burst, and the 1999 repeal of Glass-Steagall unleashed risky banking. Abroad, Clinton stood by during the Rwandan genocide but joined NATO's intervention against ethnic cleansing in the Balkans, as human rights gained prominence; at home, 1999 protesters in Seattle challenged the World Trade Organization and globalization's costs.

Post-1965 immigration meanwhile remade American society: tens of millions of newcomers, mostly from Latin America and Asia, made Latinos the largest minority and fueled 'Culture Wars' over multiculturalism, bilingualism, and family values, while incarceration soared and the 1992 Los Angeles riots exposed persistent racial injustice. Antigovernment extremism climaxed in the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing. Clinton survived impeachment over the Lewinsky affair in 1999, and in 2000 the Supreme Court's Bush v. Gore ruling halted Florida's recount, handing George W. Bush the presidency despite his loss of the popular vote. On September 11, 2001, Al Qaeda's attacks on the World Trade Center and Pentagon killed some 3,000 people and shattered America's post–Cold War sense of security.
big_ideas: The peaceful collapse of communism in 1989–1991 ended the Cold War, left the United States the sole superpower, and opened nearly the entire world to market capitalism.
The Gulf War of 1991 showcased American power in the post–Cold War order, but policymakers disagreed over whether the United States should act as a global policeman.
Clinton consolidated the conservative turn in American politics by embracing free trade, balanced budgets, and welfare abolition while defending social liberalism.
Globalization and the computer revolution drove the 1990s boom, yet deregulation, outsourcing, and speculation widened inequality and set the stage for later financial crises.
Post-1965 immigration from Latin America and Asia transformed the nation's demographics, sparking Culture Wars over multiculturalism, language, and family values.
Despite the end of legal segregation, mass incarceration, housing segregation, and the 1992 Los Angeles riots showed that racial inequality persisted.
The disputed 2000 election, settled by the Supreme Court in Bush v. Gore, revealed a nation split almost exactly in half and a democracy with troubling flaws.

key_terms.def: George H. W. Bush's phrase for the post–Cold War era, which he envisioned as organized around democracy and global free trade under American leadership.
The 1991 conflict in which a U.S.-led international coalition drove Saddam Hussein's Iraq out of Kuwait; the quick victory sent Bush's approval soaring but left Hussein in power.
The North American Free Trade Agreement, approved in 1993, which eliminated tariffs among the United States, Canada, and Mexico; unions and environmentalists warned it would export American jobs.
Newt Gingrich's 1994 Republican platform promising smaller government, tax cuts, and welfare overhaul; it helped the GOP win Congress for the first time since the 1950s.
The accelerating flow of goods, capital, people, information, and culture across national borders that defined the 1990s economy and provoked protest over its social costs.
The December 1999 demonstrations by some 30,000 labor, environmental, and human-rights activists against the World Trade Organization, which put globalization's inequities on the world's agenda.
The violent expulsion of an ethnic group from a territory, a term that entered global vocabulary during the wars following Yugoslavia's breakup, prompting NATO's 1999 intervention in Kosovo.
The 1994 slaughter of more than 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, by Hutu extremists in Rwanda while the United States and the world declined to intervene.
The 1990s battles over moral values—abortion, gay rights, school curricula, evolution, and the family—pitting religious conservatives against secular and multicultural America.
A 1990s emphasis on racial and ethnic group identity and demands that institutions reflect America's growing diversity; celebrated by some and blamed by others for national fragmentation.
A 1990 law extending the rights revolution by banning discrimination against people with disabilities in employment and requiring accessible public buildings.
The 1992 Los Angeles uprising, the deadliest since the Civil War draft riots, that erupted after police officers were acquitted in the videotaped beating of a Black motorist.
The 1995 destruction of a federal building by antigovernment extremist Timothy McVeigh, which killed 168 people and exposed the danger of far-right militia movements.
The 1998 House vote charging Clinton with perjury and obstruction of justice over his affair with Monica Lewinsky; the Senate acquitted him in 1999, and his popularity endured.
The 5-4 Supreme Court decision of December 2000 that stopped Florida's ballot recount, deciding the presidency for George W. Bush although Al Gore won the popular vote.
The terrorist network led by Osama bin Laden—angered by U.S. bases in Saudi Arabia and support for Israel—that carried out the September 11, 2001 attacks killing about 3,000 people.

timeline.event: Berlin Wall falls as communism collapses across eastern Europe; Chinese troops crush pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square.
U.S.-led coalition wins the Gulf War; the Soviet Union dissolves, ending the Cold War.
Los Angeles erupts in riots after the Rodney King verdict; Bill Clinton wins a three-way presidential race.
Congress approves NAFTA, creating a North American free-trade zone.
Republicans sweep Congress behind the Contract with America; genocide kills more than 800,000 in Rwanda.
Timothy McVeigh's bomb destroys the Oklahoma City federal building, killing 168.
Clinton signs the law abolishing AFDC welfare and wins reelection over Bob Dole.
The House impeaches Clinton over the Lewinsky scandal; the Senate acquits him in early 1999.
NATO wages war over Kosovo; Seattle protesters disrupt the WTO; Congress repeals the Glass-Steagall Act.
The Supreme Court's Bush v. Gore ruling settles the disputed election for George W. Bush.
Al Qaeda hijackers attack the World Trade Center and Pentagon on September 11, killing about 3,000 people.

themes: America in the world: The Cold War's end made the United States the sole superpower, forcing debates—from the Gulf War to Kosovo to Rwanda—over when America should intervene abroad.
Work, exchange, and technology: Computers, the Internet, and globalization powered a historic boom, but outsourcing, deregulation, and speculation deepened inequality and financial risk.

Migration and settlement: The largest immigration wave in U.S. history, overwhelmingly from Latin America and Asia, spread diversity nationwide and fueled political conflict over borders and language.
American identity: Culture Wars over multiculturalism, family values, gay rights, and religion showed Americans divided over what the nation should be.
Politics and power: Clinton's centrism ratified the conservative shift in politics, while impeachment and the razor-thin 2000 election revealed intense partisanship and a democracy under strain.
